title: Nutrition
tagline: The classes of food and their tests, the balanced diet, deficiency diseases, teeth, and human digestion.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every food class, chemical test, deficiency disease and stage of digestion below is standard human biology and nutrition. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: This chapter covers nutrition on three scales. It starts with food itself — the classes of food, the chemical tests that identify them, and what each class does in the body. It then moves to diet: what a balanced diet is, how much energy a person needs, and what happens when a nutrient is missing, described through the deficiency diseases. The final section treats the human body's own machinery, first the structure of a tooth with its dental diseases, and then the alimentary canal and its glands, following a meal from the mouth through the stomach to the small intestine, where digestion is completed and absorption takes place across the villi.

facts.value: Biuret test gives a violet colour

facts.value: Fehling's or Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate on heating

facts.value: In the small intestine, across the villi

learningOutcomes: Classify food into its major classes, state the function of each, and carry out the chemical tests that identify them.
Explain what makes a diet balanced and describe the effects of lacking a specific nutrient.
Draw and label a tooth in section, naming the tissues and the diseases that affect them.
Trace the course of a meal through the alimentary canal, naming the juices, enzymes and end products at each stage.

learn.title: Classes of food, their functions and their tests

blocks.text: Food is grouped into six classes according to what the body uses it for. Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy, yielding about four kilojoules per gram when oxidised, and they are divided into sugars, which are small and soluble, and starch, the storage form in plants made of long chains of glucose. Fats are a concentrated energy store, yielding roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, and they also insulate the body and cushion the organs. Proteins are the building and repair materials: they form the structural part of muscles, and enzymes, hormones and antibodies are all proteins, so they are essential for growth. Vitamins are organic accessories needed in very small amounts, each with a specific role, and they cannot be synthesised by the body in sufficient quantity. Minerals such as calcium, iron, iodine and phosphorus are needed for particular structures — calcium for bones and teeth, iron for haemoglobin, iodine for thyroxine. Water is the medium of all reactions and makes up a large proportion of the body, while roughage, the indigestible cellulose of plant food, adds bulk to the faeces and keeps the bowel moving. The standard chemical tests distinguish them: iodine for starch, Biuret for protein, Fehling's for reducing sugar, and a grease stain for fat.

items.meaning: A diet containing all the classes of food in the correct proportions for that person's age, size and activity.
Indigestible plant fibre that adds bulk to the residue and aids peristalsis.
Illness caused by the prolonged absence of one nutrient from the diet.
A sugar that reduces Fehling's or Benedict's solution to a brick-red precipitate on heating, such as glucose.
Breaking large fat globules into many small droplets, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.
Rhythmic wave-like contraction of circular and longitudinal muscle that pushes food along the alimentary canal.

items: Carbohydrates give quick energy; fats give more energy per gram and are stored as reserve food.
Protein is required for growth, so a growing child needs proportionally more of it than a sedentary adult.
Vitamins are organic and needed in tiny quantities; minerals are inorganic and are needed for specific structures.
Vitamin D can be made in the skin when it is exposed to sunlight, so not every vitamin must come from food.
Water forms a large proportion of the body and all digestive reactions take place in an aqueous medium.
Roughage is not absorbed and supplies no energy, yet a diet lacking it causes constipation.
Starch is a polysaccharide and is not sweet; a sugar is a monosaccharide or disaccharide and is sweet.
Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch and this is the standard test used in school practicals.

items.text: Add iodine solution to a slice of potato and it turns blue-black, while the same test on a drop of glucose solution gives no colour — the starch is present in one and not the other.
items.note: Iodine tests starch specifically; it does not detect sugar at all.

items.text: A slice of bread rubbed on paper leaves a stain that stays translucent after heating, showing fat; a crumb soaked in water leaves a mark that fades as it dries.
items.note: The persistence of the stain after heating is what distinguishes fat from water.

blocks.text: A balanced diet supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage in the proportions a particular person needs, and that proportion depends on age, body size, occupation and state of health. A growing child needs more protein for tissue building, an active labourer needs more carbohydrate for energy, and an elderly person with a lower metabolic rate generally needs less total energy. Energy requirements are normally described in terms of the calories or kilojoules needed each day, rising with physical activity. When one nutrient is chronically absent a deficiency disease develops, and each is tied to a specific missing item. Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds. Lack of vitamin D, or of calcium and vitamin D together, causes rickets in children, in which the bones soften and bend under the body's weight. Lack of vitamin B1 causes beri-beri, affecting nerves and muscles. Lack of niacin causes pellagra, and lack of vitamin A causes night blindness by depriving the eye of the pigment needed in dim light. Lack of iron reduces haemoglobin and causes anaemia; lack of iodine causes goitre by depriving the thyroid gland of the raw material for thyroxine. Protein-energy malnutrition in young children gives kwashiorkor, where muscles waste and the belly swells, and marasmus, where both protein and total energy are lacking and the child becomes emaciated.

blocks.caption: Deficiency diseases and their causes
rows: Bleeding gums, poor wound healing, capillary fragility
Soft, bowed bones in a growing child
Nerve and muscle damage; weakness and swelling
Carrot, mango, butter, fish liver oil
Enlarged thyroid gland in the neck
Wasted muscles, oedema of the belly, thin hair
Severe wasting; skin hangs in folds
A general shortage of all food

items: Kwashiorkor and marasmus differ in degree and kind: kwashiorkor is chiefly protein shortage with adequate calories, marasmus is shortage of everything.
A child with marasmus looks like an elderly person because the fat and muscle beneath the skin have both gone.
Anaemia is not simply lack of food; it is specifically a lack of iron or of the factors needed to make haemoglobin.
Goitre results from the thyroid gland enlarging as it struggles to make thyroxine without iodine.
Night blindness is one of the earliest signs of vitamin A shortage because the pigment in the retina cannot be regenerated.
Rickets bends the long bones because they are too soft to support the child's weight.
Scurvy's bleeding gums arise because collagen cannot be formed properly without vitamin C.
A balanced diet is a matter of proportion, not merely of having every food group present at some point in the week.

items.text: A child who eats only polished rice and little else develops weakness in the legs and difficulty walking within months, which is the classic presentation of beri-beri from vitamin B1 shortage.
items.note: Polishing rice removes the B1-rich outer layer, which is why the disease was once widespread in rice-eating regions.

items.text: A toddler fed on a starchy gruel with almost no protein has a swollen belly, thin arms and a pale, listless manner — the swollen abdomen distinguishing kwashiorkor from the emaciation of marasmus.
items.note: The belly swells from fluid because blood proteins, particularly albumin, cannot be made.

learn.title: The structure of a tooth and dental health

blocks.text: A tooth is divided into three regions: the crown, which projects above the gum, the constricted neck at the gum line, and the root, which sits in a socket in the jawbone. Three tissues make up its bulk. Enamel covers the crown and is the hardest substance in the body, being about ninety-six per cent mineral; it is acellular, contains no living cells or blood vessels, and cannot regenerate once it is lost, which is why a damaged enamel is permanent. Beneath it lies dentine, which makes up the main mass of the tooth and, although hard, contains microscopic tubules that transmit sensation — which is why a cavity reaching dentine causes pain. In the centre is the pulp cavity, filled with living pulp containing blood vessels, nerves and connective tissue, which nourishes the tooth and gives it sensation. The root is covered by cementum rather than enamel, and it is bound to the socket by the periodontal membrane, a fibrous layer whose collagen fibres anchor the tooth while allowing a slight give during chewing. The gum, or gingiva, covers the bone and fits round the neck of the tooth. Dental caries begins when bacteria in the mouth ferment food sugars to acid, which dissolves the enamel and then the dentine; if untreated it reaches the pulp. Gum disease arises from plaque accumulating at the gum margin and causing inflammation and recession, and it is prevented by brushing regularly, cleaning between the teeth and reducing sugary food.

items: Enamel has no cells, no nerves and no blood supply, so it cannot repair itself once destroyed.
Dentine tubules are why a cavity that has passed the enamel produces a sharp ache on cold or sweet food.
The pulp gives the tooth its blood supply and its nerve, which is why an inflamed pulp causes severe pain.
Cementum covers the root only; the crown is covered by enamel, and this difference matters in labelling.
The periodontal membrane is the reason a tooth is not rigidly fused to bone — it acts as a ligament and a shock absorber.
Dental caries is caused by acid from bacterial fermentation of sugars, not by sugar directly.
Plaque is a film of bacteria and material in which acid is held against the enamel, so brushing removes the cause.
Milk teeth need care because they are not disposable: decay in them can affect the developing permanent tooth beneath.

items.text: A sweet left against the enamel overnight lets bacteria produce acid locally, so the enamel demineralises first and the child feels nothing until the cavity reaches dentine and the tubules carry the stimulus to the pulp.
items.note: The sequence explains why pain is a late sign of decay.

items.text: Someone who brushes hard with a firm brush wears the gum back and exposes the cementum of the root, leading to sensitivity even though the enamel is intact.
items.note: Over-brushing causes gum recession, which is a different problem from caries.

blocks.text: Digestion is the chemical breakdown of complex, insoluble food into simple, soluble substances that can cross the intestinal wall, and it is carried out by the alimentary canal together with its associated glands. Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth cut and grind the food mechanically and the tongue mixes it with saliva from the three pairs of salivary glands. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which begins the digestion of starch by breaking it into the sugar maltose, and it works best in a slightly acidic to neutral medium. The bolus is swallowed and pushed down the oesophagus by peristalsis, not by gravity, into the stomach. Gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, which makes the medium strongly acidic so that pepsin can act and which kills most swallowed bacteria, plus pepsin, which begins protein digestion by breaking proteins into peptones, and mucus, which protects the stomach wall from the acid. The partly digested material, now called chyme, passes into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, where it meets bile from the liver stored in the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas. Bile contains no enzyme but emulsifies fat into small droplets, greatly increasing the surface available for digestion, and it also neutralises the acid so that the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes can work. Pancreatic juice supplies amylase, trypsin and lipase, and the intestinal juice supplies erepsin, maltase, sucrase and lactase, completing digestion to amino acids, glucose and fatty acids.

items: Digestion is entirely extracellular — the enzymes act outside the cells, in the lumen of the canal.
The small intestine is where both digestion is completed and absorption takes place, which is why it is the longest part.
Bile emulsifies but does not chemically digest fat; it only increases the surface area for lipase.
Hydrochloric acid serves two purposes: it provides the acidic pH pepsin requires and it kills swallowed microbes.
Villi are folds with a rich blood supply, a lacteal and a thin epithelium, giving a huge surface area for absorption.
Amino acids and glucose are absorbed into the blood capillaries of a villus, while the products of fat digestion enter the lacteal.
The liver processes absorbed amino acids by removing their nitrogen, which is converted to urea.
The large intestine absorbs water, so what leaves as faeces is compacted residue rather than diluted waste.
Peristalsis is a wave of circular muscle contraction behind the food with longitudinal muscle ahead of it.

items.meaning: The softened, mixed mass of food as it is swallowed from the mouth.
The semi-fluid acidic mixture of food and gastric juice as it leaves the stomach.
Physical division of fat into many small droplets by bile, increasing the area for lipase.
A finger-like fold of the small intestine wall that greatly increases the absorbing surface.
The blind lymph vessel at the centre of a villus that absorbs the products of fat digestion.
Rhythmic muscular waves that propel food along the canal.
Removal of undigested residue from the body; not an excretory process.

items.text: A slice of bread chewed slowly begins to taste sweet before it is swallowed, because salivary amylase has already begun breaking the starch into maltose while the food is still in the mouth.
items.note: Digestion of starch starts in the mouth, not in the stomach.

items.text: A person with a blocked bile duct cannot emulsify fat properly, so fatty foods pass through undigested and leave the stool pale and bulky, showing that bile is needed even though it contains no enzyme.
items.note: The absence of enzyme does not mean absence of function.

figures.caption: Figure: A mammalian tooth in section
figures.description: A longitudinal section through a molar showing three regions labelled crown, neck and root. The crown is capped by a thick white layer of enamel. Beneath it the bulk of the tooth is dentine, shown in a different tone and marked with fine tubules. In the centre a narrow pulp cavity runs down the root canals, filled with pulp and carrying a blood vessel and a nerve. The root is covered by cementum and held in a bony socket by the fibres of the periodontal membrane, with the gum fitting round the neck.
labels: blood vessel and nerve in the pulp

figures.caption: Figure: The human alimentary canal
figures.description: A continuous outline running from the mouth to the anus with the organs labelled in order. The mouth shows teeth and the salivary glands opening into it; the oesophagus descends to a J-shaped stomach; the liver and gall bladder sit above a coiled small intestine whose first loop is the duodenum; the pancreas opens into the duodenum; the large intestine frames the small intestine with the caecum and appendix at one corner; and the rectum and anus close the canal at the bottom.

figures.caption: Figure: A villus in the small intestine wall
figures.description: A single finger-like villus magnified from the intestinal wall, with a cut-away showing its interior. A network of blood capillaries runs through it and is drained by a vein, while a central blind-ended lacteal sits in the middle. The epithelium covering the villus is drawn as a single layer of columnar cells with a striated border, and arrows show amino acids and glucose entering the capillary while the products of fat digestion enter the lacteal.

keyPoints: Food falls into six classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water, with roughage as the indigestible fraction.
Carbohydrates give quick energy, fats store concentrated energy, proteins build and repair tissue.
Starch is tested with iodine giving blue-black; protein with the Biuret test giving violet; reducing sugar with Fehling's giving brick-red on heating; fat by a permanent translucent paper stain.
A balanced diet provides every class in the proportions right for the person's age, size and activity.
Scurvy is vitamin C, rickets is vitamin D with calcium, beri-beri is vitamin B1, night blindness is vitamin A.
Anaemia is iron shortage and goitre is iodine shortage; kwashiorkor is protein shortage and marasmus a shortage of everything.
Enamel covers the crown and is acellular and cannot regenerate; dentine contains tubules; the pulp holds the vessels and nerves.
Caries is caused by acid from bacterial fermentation of sugars, and it is the acid, not the sugar itself, that dissolves enamel.
Digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase acting on starch, and the protein-digesting pepsin works only in the acid of the stomach.
Bile emulsifies fat without digesting it, and all digestion is completed and absorbed in the small intestine across the villi.
examFocus: The food tests need reagent and result together — iodine turning blue-black, Fehling's giving a brick-red precipitate on heating — because the colour without the reagent loses the mark.
For deficiency diseases always name the disease, the specific nutrient and one symptom; the symptom is what distinguishes scurvy from rickets in an examiner's mind.
A tooth diagram must show enamel, dentine, pulp and cementum correctly placed, and must not label the root as covered by enamel.
Digestion answers should be organised organ by organ in order, naming the juice, the enzyme and the end product at each stage.
Do not say bile digests fat. It emulsifies, which is a physical change that gives lipase more surface to act on.

Illness arising from the prolonged lack of one nutrient in the diet.
Indigestible fibre that adds bulk and aids the passage of residue.

Wave-like muscular contractions that push food along the alimentary canal.

Passage of undigested residue out of the body.

questions.prompt: Which reagent is used to test for starch, and what colour indicates its presence?
options: Fehling's solution, brick red on heating
questions.explanation: Iodine solution is yellow-brown by itself and turns blue-black in the presence of starch, which is the standard school test performed on foods such as potato or bread. Fehling's detects reducing sugar, the Biuret test detects protein, and Sudan stains fat.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing iodine and Fehling's. Iodine is for starch and Fehling's is for reducing sugar, and both are commonly recalled the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: The hardest substance in the human body is __________, which covers the __________ of the tooth and contains no living cells.
questions.explanation: Enamel is about ninety-six per cent mineral, making it the hardest substance in the body, and it is acellular — it has no cells, nerves or blood supply, so it cannot repair itself once lost. It covers the crown of the tooth; the root is covered instead by cementum.
questions.commonMistake: Saying enamel covers the whole tooth. It is restricted to the crown, and the root is covered by cementum.

questions.prompt: A child has soft, bowed legs, poor muscle tone and is reluctant to walk. Which deficiency is most likely?
options: Scurvy from lack of vitamin C
Rickets from lack of vitamin D and calcium
Night blindness from lack of vitamin A
questions.answer: Rickets from lack of vitamin D and calcium
questions.explanation: Rickets is the failure of bones to harden properly in a growing child, for want of vitamin D or calcium or both, so the long bones bend under the body's weight and the child resists standing. Scurvy causes bleeding gums, night blindness affects vision in dim light, and goitre gives a swelling in the neck.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing scurvy because it also involves bones and teeth. Scurvy affects collagen and gives bleeding gums, not bowed legs.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a balanced diet, and why do the requirements of a growing child and an elderly adult differ?
questions.answer: A balanced diet is one that supplies carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage in the correct proportions for the particular individual. A growing child needs proportionally more protein, because tissue is being built rapidly and proteins are the material of growth and repair, together with enough calcium and vitamin D for the developing skeleton. An elderly adult is generally less active and has a lower metabolic rate, so the total energy requirement from carbohydrate and fat is lower, while the need for protective nutrients such as vitamins and minerals remains.
questions.explanation: Both parts are required: what balance means, and why the proportions change with age. The key distinction is growth against maintenance, since protein demand is driven by building new tissue while energy demand is driven by activity.
questions.commonMistake: Equating a balanced diet with eating a large quantity of everything. Balance is about proportion to the individual, not abundance.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a tooth under its three regions, naming the tissues present and the function of each.
questions.answer: A tooth is divided into the crown, which projects above the gum and performs the cutting and crushing of food, the neck, a slight constriction at the level of the gum where crown and root meet, and the root, which is embedded in a socket in the jaw bone and anchors the tooth. Three tissues make up its substance. Enamel covers the crown; it is the hardest substance in the body, is acellular and translucent, and protects the tooth against wear, acid and temperature, but it cannot regenerate because it contains no living cells. Dentine forms the bulk of the tooth beneath the enamel and in the root; it is hard but contains fine tubules that transmit sensation, which is why a cavity reaching it causes pain. In the centre lies the pulp cavity, filled with living pulp carrying blood vessels, nerves and connective tissue that nourish the tooth and give it sensation. The root is covered by cementum rather than enamel, and the tooth is held in its socket by the fibres of the periodontal membrane.
questions.explanation: The answer must give the three regions and the three principal tissues with a function attached to each. The distinction between enamel on the crown and cementum on the root is a frequent source of error, and stating that enamel cannot regenerate explains why prevention matters.
questions.commonMistake: Labelling the root as covered by enamel. Cementum covers the root, and this is one of the most commonly lost marks in tooth diagrams.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the action of bile is correct?
options: Bile contains lipase and digests fat into fatty acids
Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets and neutralises the acid from the stomach
Bile digests protein into peptides in the stomach
Bile is produced by the gall bladder and contains amylase
questions.answer: Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets and neutralises the acid from the stomach
questions.explanation: Bile contains no enzyme. It breaks large fat globules into many small droplets, giving lipase a far larger surface to act on, and it is alkaline, so it cancels the acidity of the chyme and creates the pH that pancreatic and intestinal enzymes require. Lipase comes from the pancreas rather than from bile, and the liver makes bile while the gall bladder stores it.
questions.commonMistake: Saying bile contains lipase. Emulsification is a physical change, and the enzyme that digests fat comes from the pancreas.

questions.prompt: Describe the digestion of a starchy, slightly fatty meal from the mouth to the point where absorption takes place, naming the organ, the juice, the enzyme and the end product at each stage.
questions.answer: In the mouth the teeth grind the food mechanically and it is mixed with saliva, whose enzyme salivary amylase hydrolyses starch into the sugar maltose, working best near neutrality. The bolus is swallowed and moved by peristalsis down the oesophagus to the stomach, where gastric juice supplies hydrochloric acid and pepsin; the acid activates pepsin and kills microbes, and pepsin begins protein digestion by breaking proteins into peptones, while mucus protects the stomach wall. The chyme enters the duodenum, where bile from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, emulsifies the fat into fine droplets and neutralises the acid. Pancreatic juice then adds amylase to continue starch digestion, trypsin to continue protein digestion, and lipase to digest the emulsified fat. Finally the intestinal juice, containing erepsin, maltase, sucrase and lactase, completes digestion so that the products are amino acids from protein, glucose from maltose and other sugars, and fatty acids and glycerol from fat. These simple soluble products are then absorbed across the epithelium of the villi of the small intestine into the blood capillaries and the lacteal.
questions.explanation: The answer must be a continuous sequence with four elements at each stage — organ, juice, enzyme and product — since omitting any one leaves the chain incomplete. The two roles of bile, emulsifying and neutralising, must both appear, and the final step must name the villi as the site of absorption.
questions.commonMistake: Stating that digestion of starch finishes in the mouth. Salivary amylase begins it there, but the acid of the stomach stops its action and it resumes with pancreatic amylase in the small intestine.

questions.prompt: State the causes of dental caries and of gum disease, and describe two measures that prevent them.
questions.answer: Dental caries is caused by acids produced when bacteria living in plaque ferment sugars left on the tooth; the acid dissolves the enamel and, if the decay continues, penetrates the dentine and may reach the pulp. Gum disease arises when plaque accumulates along the margin of the gum, causing inflammation, recession of the gum and eventually loosening of the teeth. Two preventive measures are to brush regularly, at least twice a day and particularly after sweet food, which removes plaque before the bacteria can act, and to reduce the frequency of sugary food and drink in the diet, since it is repeated exposure to sugar rather than the total amount that gives bacteria prolonged opportunity to produce acid. Cleaning between the teeth with floss and attending for professional cleaning are further measures.
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be explained by their mechanism — acid for caries, plaque at the gum margin for gum disease — since naming them without cause earns little. The preventive measures must act on that mechanism: removing the plaque, or removing the substrate the bacteria ferment.
questions.commonMistake: Saying sugar rots the teeth. Sugar itself does not dissolve enamel; the acid produced by bacteria fermenting it does.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin deficiency causes bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is required for the formation of collagen, the protein that holds tissues together and gives capillaries their strength. Without it the gums bleed, old wounds reopen and new ones heal poorly, which is scurvy. Vitamin A affects vision in dim light, vitamin B1 causes beri-beri, and vitamin D is needed for calcium deposition in bone.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing vitamin D because it is associated with teeth and gums. Vitamin D concerns calcium and bone hardening, not collagen and bleeding.

questions.prompt: Absorption of the products of digestion takes place across the __________ of the small intestine, while the products of fat digestion enter the central __________ of each one.
questions.explanation: The villi are finger-like folds that greatly increase the absorbing surface of the small intestine, are covered by a single layer of cells and carry a rich blood supply, which keeps the concentration gradient steep. Amino acids and glucose pass into the blood capillaries, while the fatty acids and glycerol, having been recombined, enter the blind lymph vessel at the centre called the lacteal.
questions.commonMistake: Saying all products enter the blood. Fat-soluble products go into the lacteal, which is why fatty food is absorbed into the lymphatic system first.

questions.prompt: A person's diet consists almost entirely of polished rice with a little sugar and no pulses, milk, vegetables or fruit. Identify two likely deficiency conditions, state the nutrient missing in each case, and explain why a diet that supplies enough energy can still be inadequate.
questions.answer: First, anaemia is likely, because the diet provides little or no iron; iron is required to make haemoglobin, so its shortage reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and produces fatigue and pallor. Second, scurvy is likely, because there is no fruit or vegetable to supply vitamin C, which is needed for collagen formation, so the gums would become spongy and bleed and wounds would heal slowly. Beri-beri is also a risk if the rice is heavily polished, since polishing removes vitamin B1. The diet can supply adequate energy because polished rice and sugar are rich in carbohydrate, which oxidises to release plenty of kilojoules, yet energy is only one of the requirements of the body: proteins are needed for growth and repair, minerals for haemoglobin and bones, and vitamins to regulate the chemical processes that release and use that energy. A person may therefore eat enough to feel full and to maintain weight while still lacking the materials needed for normal structure and function, which is exactly what is meant by hidden hunger.
questions.explanation: Two deficiency diseases must be named with their missing nutrients, and the final part demands an argument distinguishing energy supply from nutritional adequacy — carbohydrate provides fuel, but fuel without vitamins, minerals and protein does not maintain health.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing kwashiorkor for the first condition because protein is absent. That is a fair answer too, but the question asks for two conditions, and scurvy or anaemia from the missing fruit and vegetables is the clearer second identification.
